ABOUT THE AUTHORS

 

Vivian Siahaan is a fast-learner who likes to do new things. She was born, raised in Hinalang Bagasan, Balige, on the banks of Lake Toba, and completed high school education from SMAN 1 Balige. She started herself learning Java, Android, JavaScript, CSS, C ++, Python, R, Visual Basic, Visual C #, MATLAB, Mathematica, PHP, JSP, MySQL, SQL Server, Oracle, Access, and other programming languages. She studied programming from scratch, starting with the most basic syntax and logic, by building several simple and applicable GUI applications. Animation and games are fields of programming that are interests that she always wants to develop. Besides studying mathematical logic and programming, the author also has the pleasure of reading novels. Vivian Siahaan has written dozens of ebooks that have been published on Sparta Publisher: Data Structure with Java; Java Programming: Cookbook; C ++ Programming: Cookbook; C Programming For High Schools / Vocational Schools and Students; Java Programming for SMA / SMK; Java Tutorial: GUI, Graphics and Animation; Visual Basic Programming: From A to Z; Java Programming for Animation and Games; C # Programming for SMA / SMK and Students; MATLAB For Students and Researchers; Graphics in JavaScript: Quick Learning Series; JavaScript Image Processing Methods: From A to Z; Java GUI Case Study: AWT & Swing; Basic CSS and JavaScript; PHP / MySQL Programming: Cookbook; Visual Basic: Cookbook; C ++ Programming for High Schools / Vocational Schools and Students; Concepts and Practices of C ++; PHP / MySQL For Students; C # Programming: From A to Z; Visual Basic for SMA / SMK and Students; C # .NET and SQL Server for High School / Vocational School and Students. Rismon Hasiholan Sianipar was born in Pematang Siantar, in 1994. After graduating from SMAN 3 Pematang Siantar 3, the writer traveled to the city of Jogjakarta. In 1998 and 2001 the author completed his Bachelor of Engineering (S.T) and Master of Engineering (M.T) education in the Electrical Engineering of Gadjah Mada University, under the guidance of Prof. Dr. Adhi Soesanto and Prof. Dr. Thomas Sri Widodo, focusing on research on non-stationary signals by analyzing their energy using time-frequency maps. Because of its non-stationary nature, the distribution of signal energy becomes very dynamic on a time-frequency map. By mapping the distribution of energy in the time-frequency field using discrete wavelet transformations, one can design non-linear filters so that they can analyze the pattern of the data contained in it. In 2003, the author received a Monbukagakusho scholarship from the Japanese Government. In 2005 and 2008, he completed his Master of Engineering (M.Eng) and Doctor of Engineering (Dr.Eng) education at Yamaguchi University, under the guidance of Prof. Dr. Hidetoshi Miike. Both the master's thesis and his doctoral thesis, R.H. Sianipar combines SR-FHN (Stochastic Resonance Fitzhugh-Nagumo) filter strength with cryptosystem ECC (elliptic curve cryptography) 4096-bit both to suppress noise in digital images and digital video and maintain its authenticity. The results of this study have been documented in international scientific journals and officially patented in Japan. One of the patents was published in Japan with a registration number 2008-009549.

Aside from being an active writer teaching in the Electrical Engineering University of Mataram, he is also active in collaborating with several universities and research institutions in Japan, particularly in the fields of cryptography, cryptanalysis and audio / image / video digital forensics. R.H. Sianipar also has experience in conducting code-breaking methods (cryptanalysis) on a number of intelligence data that are the object of research studies in Japan. R.H. Sianipar has a number of Japanese patents, and has written a number of national / international scientific articles, and dozens of national books. R.H. Sianipar has also participated in a number of workshops related to cryptography, cryptanalysis, digital watermarking, and digital forensics. In a number of workshops, R.H. Sianipar helps Prof. Hidetoshi Miike to create applications related to digital image / video processing, steganography, cryptography, watermarking, non-linear screening, intelligent descriptor-based computer vision, and others, which are used as training materials. Field of interest in the study of R.H. Sianipar is multimedia security, signal processing / digital image / video, cryptography, digital communication, digital forensics, and data compression / coding. Until now, R.H. Sianipar continues to develop applications related to analysis of signal, image, and digital video, both for research purposes and for commercial purposes based on the Python programming language, MATLAB, C ++, C, VB.NET, C # .NET, R, and Java.

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

ABOUT THE BOOK

 

 

In chapter one, you will learn to know the properties and events of each control in a Windows Visual C# application. You need to learn and know in order to be more familiar when applying them to some applications in this book.

 

In chapter two, you will build a project so that children can practice basic skills in addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division operations. This Math Game project can be used to choose the types of questions and what factors you want to use. This project has three timing options. Random math problems using values ​​from 0 to 9 will be presented. Timing options are provided to measure accuracy and speed. There are many controls used. Two label controls are used for title information, two for displaying scores. There is a wide label in the middle of the form to display math questions. And, long skinny label is used as separator. Two button controls are used to start and stop question and one button to exit the project. There are three group control boxes. The first group box holds four check box controls that are used to select the type of questions. The second group box holds eleven radio buttons that are used to select values ​​that are used as factors in calculations. The third group box contains three radio button controls for timing options. A scroll bar control rod is used to change the time.

 

In chapter three, you will build Bank Code game. The storage box is locked and can only be opened if you enter the correct digit combination. Combinations can be 2 to 4 non-repetitive digits (range of digits from 1 to 9). After a guess is given, you will be notified of how many digits are right and how many digits are in the right position. Based on this information, you will give another guess. You continue to guess until you get the right combination or until you stop the game. On the left side of the form is a large picture box control. On the right side, two group box controls and two button controls are placed. In the picture box, a control panel is placed. In the panel, there are four label controls (set the AutoSize property to False ) and nine button controls. In the first group box control, place three radio buttons. In the second group box control, a text box control is placed. The picture box contains an image of bank and a panel. The label controls in the panel are used to display the combinations entered (the BorderStyle property set to FixedSingle to display the label size). The nine buttons on the panel are used to enter combinations. Radio buttons are used to set options. The buttons (one to start and stop the game and another to exit the project) are used to control game operations. The text box displays the results of the combinations entered.

 

In chapter four, you will build Horse Racing game. This is a simple game. Up to 10 horses will race to the finish line. You guessed two horses that you thought could win the race. By clicking on the Start button, the race will start. All horses will race speed to get to the finish line. Labels are used to display instructions and number of horses in a race. Four button controls are used: two buttons to change number of horses, one button to start the game, and one other button to stop the game. The picture box control is used to load the horse image. A timer control is used to update the horse's movement during the race.

 

In chapter five, you will build Catching Ball game. The bird flew and dropped ball from the sky. Users are challenged to position man under the fallen ball to catch it. Labels are used for instructions and to display game information (remaining time, number of balls captured, and game difficulty level). Two buttons are used to change the game difficulty level, one button to start the game, and another button to stop the game. Picture box controls hold images for man, bird, and ball.

 

In chapter six, you will build Smart Tic Tac Toe game. That said, this is the first game ever programmed on a computer and one that had been programmed by Bill Gates himself when he was a teenager while attending Lakeside School in Seattle. The aim of this game is to win the game on a 3 x 3 grid with the victory of three identical symbols (X or O) on horizontal, diagonal, or vertical lines. The players will play alternately. In this game given two game options: player 1 against player 2 or human player against computer. A smart but simple strategy will be developed for computer logic to be a formidable opponent for humans.

 

In chapter seven, you will build Fighting Plane program. This program can be played by two human players or human player versus computer. The controls of the player are done via the keyboard. Player 1 presses A key to move up, Z key to move down, and S key to throw rudal. When you choose Two players from the Options button, this game can be played by two human players. Player 1 presses the same keys, while player 2 presses key K to move up, M to move down, and key J to throw rudal. All label controls are used for titles and provide scoring and game information. The large panel (Panel1) is the playing field. Three button controls are used to start / stop a program, set options, and exit the program. One timer control is used to control game animation and another is used to represent the computer's decision process. The second control panel (Panel2) is used to select game options. One group box contains radio buttons which are used to select number of players. A group box contains radio buttons to select the level of difficulty of the game, when playing against a computer. A small button is used to close the options panel. The default properties are set for one-player games with the easiest game difficulty.

TUTORIAL 1

VISUAL C# CONTROLS

 

 

In this chapter, you will learn to know the properties and events of each control in a Windows Visual C# application. You need to learn and know in order to be more familiar when applying them to some applications in this book.

 

 

Form

Forms are objects where the user interface is designed. The form is also known as a container or loader object, because it contains other controls. A number of controls are placed on the form having BackColor , ForeColor , and Font properties. To change it, you can select the desired control (after it is placed in the form) and change the desired properties. Another feature of this container control is that when Enable property is False , all controls on that form will be deactivated. Likewise, when this container control has a Visible property of False , then all controls on the form become invisible.

 

Here, a number of properties, methods, and events commonly used for forms will be presented. Recall that the property describes the appearance and value of a control, a method is an action or task performed by a control, and an event occurs when something is done to that control.

 

Following are the properties of the Form :

 

Table 1.1 A number of properties of the Form object

Name

Used to get or set the form name.

AcceptButton

Used to get or set button that is clicked on form when user presses the ENTER key.

BackColor

Used to get or set the background color of the form.

CancelButton

Used to get or set button that is clicked on form when user presses the Esc key.

ControlBox

Used to get or set a value that indicates whether a control box is displayed on the caption bar of the form.

Enabled

If it is False , all controls on the form will be disabled.

Font

Used to get or set font name, size, and style.

ForeColor

Used to get or set the color of text or graphics.

FormBorderStyle

Used to set form boundaries to be fixed or dynamic.

Height

Form height in pixel.

Help

Used to get or set a value that indicates whether the Help button needs to be displayed or not.

Icon

Used to get or set an icon for a form.

Left

Distance from the left of the screen to the left edge of the form, in pixel.

MaximizeButton

Used to get or set a value that indicates whether the maximized button is displayed on the caption bar of the form.

MinimizeButton

Used to get or set a value that indicates whether the minimized button is displayed on the caption bar of the form.

StartPosition

Used to get or set the initial position of the form when the application is run.

Text

Used to get or set the form window title.

Top

Distance from the top of the screen to the top edge of the form, in pixel.

Width

Form width in pixel.

 

The general syntax for calling a method is to write the name of the control, a dot, and then the method name. For the methods of the Form object, the name of the form used is this . This is a Visual C# keyword that is used to refer to a form. So, to close a form, you use: this.Close () .

 

Following are a number of methods defined for the Form object:

 

Table 1.2 A number of methods from the Form object

Close

Close the form.

Focus

Set the focus on the form.

Hide

Hide the form.

Refresh

Force the form to be displayed again.

Show

Set the Visible property as True .

 

Following are a number of Event procedures that are defined for the Form object:

 

Table 1.3 A number of Event Procedures from the Form object

Activated

Occurs when the form is activated in the code or by the user.

Click

Occurs when the form is clicked by the user.

FormClosing

Occurs when the form is closed.

DoubleClick

Occurs when the form is double clicked.

Load

Occurs when a form is displayed for the first time.

Paint

Occurs when a form is reloaded.

 

General uses of Form objects:

  • Set the Name and Text properties.
  • Set the StartPosition property, for example, to CenterScreen value.
  • Set the FormBorderStyle property to a certain value such as Fixed3D or Sizable .
  • Write down the initialization code needed in the Load event of the form. To access this event in the code window, double-click on the form.
  • Write the finalization code in the FormClosing event of the form.

Button

The Button control is probably the most commonly used Visual C# control. This control is used to start, interrupt, or end certain processes. The following will be presented a number of properties, methods, and events for button control.

 

Table 1.4 A number of properties of the Button object

Name

Used to get or set a Button object name.

BackColor

Used to get or set the background color of the button.

Enabled

If it is False , the button becomes visible, but it cannot accept clicks from user.

Font

Used to get or set font name, size, and style.

ForeColor

Used to get or set the color of text or graphics.

Image

Used to get or set the image to be displayed on the button control.

Text

Used to get or set the text or string displayed on the button.

TextAlign

Used to get or set text alignment on Button control.

 

 

Table 1.5 A number of methods of Button object

Focus

Used to assign focus to the button.

PerformClick

Generates a Click event for a button.

 

Table 1.6 The most popular event of Button object

Click

This event is triggered when the button is selected by clicking on it or by pressing the access key.

 

General uses of Button control:

  • Set the Name and Text properties.
  • Write the code in the Click event.
  • You can also change the Font , Backcolor , and Forecolor properties.

 

 

Label

The Label control is used to display text, which the user cannot edit directly. The text on a label can only be changed when the program is run when responding to an event.

 

The following will be presented a number of properties, methods, and events for label control.

 

Table 1.7 A number of properties of the Label object

Name

Used to get or set a Lable object name.

AutoSize

Used to get or set a value that indicates whether the label automatically changes size or not. The default value is True .

BackColor

Used to get or set background color on label.

BorderStyle

Used to get or set edge style for label.

Font

Used to get or set the name, style, and size of the font.

ForeColor

Used to get or set the color of text or graphics.

Text

Used to get or set the string displayed on the label.

TextAlign

Used to get or set text alignment on label.

 

Note, by default, label control cannot be resized. To do this, set the AutoSize property to False .

 

Table 1.8 One of methods of Label object

Refresh

Force an update to the content of a Label control.

 

 

Table 1.9 A number of Event Procedures from the Label object

Click

Triggered when the user clicks on a label.

DblClick

Triggered when the user double clicks on a label.

 

Common uses of Label controls:

  • Set the Name and Text properties.
  • Set the Font , BackColor , and ForeColor properties.
  • Set the AutoSize property to False and choose the desired value for TextAlign .

 

 

Timer

The Timer control in Visual C# can generate events without any input from the user. This timer control works behind the scenes on your project, which results in events with the time interval you set. This event generation feature is very helpful when the screen wants to be updated at regular time intervals.

 

The following will be presented a number of properties and event of the Timer control.

 

Table 1.10 A number of properties of the Timer object

Name

Used to get or set a Timer object name.

Enabled

Used to enable and disable timer. When the value is True , this timer control continues operations until the Enabled property is False .

Interval

Milliseconds (there are 1000 milliseconds in one second) between each Tick event call from the timer control.

 

Table 1.11 One of events of Timer object

Tick

This event procedure is called every interval (milliseconds) when the Enabled property is True .

To use the Timer control, you add it to your application like other controls. This control will be placed in the area below the form in the design window.

 

The Enabled property of the timer control is False at design time. You enable a timer in the code by changing this property to True .

 

Common uses of the Timer control:

  • Set the Name property and the Interval property.
  • Write the code in the Tick event.
  • At some point in your application, set the Enabled property to True to start the timer. You can also make it False to stop the timer.

 

 

TextBox

The TextBox control is used to display information entered at the time of design, by user when the program is run, or by code in the program.

 

Table 1.12 A number of properties of the TextBox object

Name

Get or set the name of the text box.

AutoSize

Get or set a value that indicates whether the height of the text box automatically adjusts when the font in the control changes.

BackColor

Get or set the background color from the text box.

BorderStyle

Get or set the edge style of the text box.

Font

Get or set font name, style, and size.

ForeColor

Get or set the color of text or graphics.

HideSelection

Get or set a value that indicates whether the selected text in the text box control is still highlighted when the control loses focus.

Lines

Get or set a line of text in a text box control.

MaxLength

Get or set the maximum number of characters that a user can type in the text box control.

MultiLine

Get or set a value that indicates whether the text box can contain multi-line text.

PasswordChar

Get or set character to disguise password characters in a one-line TextBox control.

ReadOnly

Get or set a value that indicates whether the text in the text box control is read-only.

ScrollBars

Get or set which scroll bars are displayed without the multi-line text box control.

SelectedText

Get or set a value that indicates the text being selected.

SelectionLength

Get or set how many characters that are selected in the text box.

SelectionStart

Get or set the starting point of the selected text in the text box.

Tag

Stores a string expression.

Text

Get or set the current text in the text box.

TextAlign

Get or set text alignment on text box.

TextLength

Get the length of the text in the text box.

 

Table 1.13 A number of methods of the TextBox object

AppendText

Append text to currentvtext in the text box.

Clear

Clear all text in the text box.

Copy

Copy selected text to the clipboard.

Cut

Move selected text to the clipboard.

Focus

Put the cursor on the specified text box.

Paste

Replace the current selection in the text box with the content of the Clipboard.

SelectAll

Select all text in the text box.

Undo

Cancel the last edit operation of the text box.

 

 

Table 1.14 A number of Events from the TextBox object

Click

Occurs when the user clicks on the text box.

Enter

Occurs when the control receives focus.

KeyDown

Occurs when a key is pressed when the control has focus.

KeyPress

Occurs when a key is pressed when the control has focus.

Leave

Triggered when the user leaves the text box. This is a way to check the content of a text box when editing the text box is done.

TextChanged

Occurs when the value of the Text property has changed.

 

General uses of the TextBox control as a viewer control:

  • Set the Name property. Initialize the Text property with the desired string.
  • Set the ReadOnly property to True .
  • If used to display text more than one line, set the MultiLine property to True .
  • You can also change the Font , BackColor , and ForeColor properties.

 

General uses of TextBox control as input device:

  • Set the Name property. Initialize the Text property with the desired string.
  • If used to display text more than one line, set the MultiLine property to True .
  • In the code, give Focus to the control when needed.
  • Provide the key entrapment code for the KeyPress event that will be discussed in this chapter.
  • Read the Text property when the Leave event occurs.
  • You can also change the Font , BackColor , and ForeColor properties.

 

 

CheckBox

Visual C# has many controls that give users many choices just by clicking the mouse. These controls are attractive, familiar, and minimize the possibility of errors in your application. You will use a lot of these controls.

 

CheckBox control provides a way to provide a selection of a number of potential choices. CheckBox is used in many Windows applications.

 

Table 1.15 A number of properties of the CheckBox object

Name

Get or set the name of the check box.

BackColor

Get or set the background color from the check box.

Checked

Get or set a value indicating whether the check box is checked.

Font

Get or set font name, style, and size.

ForeColor

Get or set the color of text or graphics.

Text

Get or set the string displayed next to the check box.

TextAlign

Get or set text alignment in the checkbox.

 

Table 1.16 One of methods of CheckBox object

Focus

Move focus to a specific check box.

 

Table 1.17 A number of Events of the CheckBox object

CheckedChanged

Occurs when the value of the Checked property changes, whether via code or when the check box is clicked.

Click

Triggered when a check box is clicked. The Checked property is automatically changed by Visual C#.

 

When a check box is clicked, if there is no check mark there ( Checked = False ), then Visual C# will place a check mark there and set Checked property to True . If clicked and previously there was a check mark there ( Checked = True ), then the check mark will disappear and Checked property will be changed to Flase .

 

General uses of CheckBox control:

  • Set the Name and Text properties.
  • Initialize the Checked property.
  • Monitor the Click or CheckChanged event to determine whether the check box is checked.
  • Change Font , BackColor , and ForeColor properties.

 

 

RadioButton

RadioButton control provides the capability to make mutually exclusive choices from a number of candidate choices. This means that the radio button works as a group, only one button can be selected. The radio button is widely used in Windows applications. Named as a radio button because it looks similar to a button on a transistor radio.

 

Following are a number of properties, methods, and events of the RadioButton control:

 

Table 1.18 A number of Properties of the RadioButton object

Name

Get or set the name of the radio button.

BackColor

Get or set the background color from the radio button.

Checked

Get or set a value indicating whether the radio button is selected.

Font

Get or set font name, style, and size.

ForeColor

Get or set the color of text or graphics.

TextAlign

Get or set text alignment on radio buttons.

 

Table 1.19 A number of Methods of the RadioButton object

Focus

Move focus to the specified radio button.

PerformClick

Generates a Click event for a particular radio button, by simulating a click by the user.

 

Table 1.20 A number of Events of the RadioButton object

CheckedChanged

Occurs when the value of the Checked property changes, whether via a code or when the radio button is clicked.

Click

Triggered when a radio button is clicked. The Checked property is automatically changed by Visual C#.

 

General uses of RadioButton control:

  • Create a radio button group.
  • For each button in a group, set the Name and Text properties.
  • Initialize the Checked property.
  • Monitor the Click or CheckChanged event on each radio button to determine which radio button is clicked.

 

 

GroupBox

You already knew that check boxes and radio buttons work in a group. The GroupBox control provides a way to group related controls in a Visual C# application.

 

To place controls in a group box, you first need to drag or place GroupBox control into the form. Then, place each control into the group box.

 

The group box affects how the radio button works. The radio buttons on a GroupBox control work as a group, and are not related to the radio buttons on other GroupBox controls.

 

Table 1.21 A number of Properties of the GroupBox object

Name

Get or set the name of the group box.

Enabled

Get or set a value indicating whether the group box is enabled. If it is False , then all controls in the group box will be disabled.

BackColor

Get or set the background color from the group box.

Font

Get or set font name, style, and size.

ForeColor

Get or set color of text.

Text

Get or set the string to be displayed in the title section of the group box.

Visible

If it is False , it will hide the group box (and all the controls it contains).

 

The GroupBox control has a number of methods and events, but all of them are rarely used. You will focus more on the methods and events associated with the controls in the group box.

 

General uses of GroupBox control:

  • Set Text and Name properties.
  • Place the desired controls in the group box.
  • Monitor the events of each control in the group box.

 

 

PictureBox

Visual C# offers a number of features for graphics. The PictureBox control is one of the main tools in exploiting these features. The picture box control can display graphic files (with various formats) and it can utilize a number of graphic functions and can be used for animation.

 

Table 1.22 A number of Properties of the PictureBox object

Name

Get or set the name of the picture box.

BackColor

Get or set the background color from the picture box.

BorderStyle

Indicate the edge style for the picture box.

Height

Heighy of the picture box in pixels.

Image

Set the graphic file to display in the picture box.

Left

The distance from the left edge of the form to the left edge of the picture box, in pixels.

SizeMode

Indicats how the picture is displayed.

Top

Lower edge distance from the area of ​​the form title to the top edge of the picture box, in pixels.

Width

Width of the picture box in pixels.

 

Table 1.23 One of Events of the PictureBox object

Click

Triggered when a picture box is clicked.

 

The Image property specifies the graphic file to be displayed. The five types of graphics files that can be placed in the image box are as follows:

 

Table 1.24 A number of acceptable graphic file types of PictureBox control

Bitmap

An image is represented by pixels and stored as a collection that contains bits. This is the format most commonly used by scanner and paintbrush programs. Format has a .bmp extension.

Icon

A special type of bitmap file with a maximum size of 32 x 32 pixels. This format has the .ico extension. The icon is used to represent Windows applications.

Metafile

A file that stores an image as a collection that contains graphical objects (lines, circles, polygons), not pixels. Metafile has a more accurate resolution than bitmaps when the size is enlarged or reduced. This format has a .wmf extension.

JPEG

JPEG (Joint Photographic Experts Group) is a compressed BMP format that supports 8 bits and 24 bit colors. This format is popular on the Internet and is a common format for digital cameras. JPEG format has the extension .jpg.

GIF

GIF (Graphic Interchange Format) is a compressed bmp format originally developed by CompuServe. This format supports up to 256 bit colors and is also popular on the Internet. This format has a .gif extension.

 

The SizeMode property states how a particular image will be displayed. There are five values ​​that can be given to this property: Normal , CenterImage , StretchImage , AutoSize , and Zoom . The effect of each of these values ​​is as follows:

 

Value of SizeMode

Effect

Normal

The image is displayed at the initial size. If the picture box is larger than the image, there will be free space. If the picture box is smaller than the image, the image will be truncated.

CenterImage

The image is displayed at its initial size, centered on the picture box. If the picture box is larger than the image, there will be free space. If the picture box is smaller than the image, the image will be truncated.

StretchImage

The image will 'fill' the picture box. If the image is smaller than the picture box, the image will expand. If the image is larger than the picture box, the image will shrink.

AutoSize

The opposite of StretchImage . The picture box will change its dimensions to adjust the initial size of the image.

Zoom

Same with StretchImage . The image will adjust so it can be loaded in the picture box.

 

Note that the dimensions remain unchanged for the Normal , CenterImage , StretchImage , and Zoom values. With AutoSize , the picture box will change size. This causes problems when the program runs if your form is not large enough to load the picture box.

 

General uses of the PicureBox control in displaying images:

  • Set the Name and SizeMode properties (often with a StretchImage value).
  • Specifiy the Image property, both at the time of design and when the program runs (run-time).

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

TUTORIAL 2

MATH GAME

 

In this tutorial, you will build a project so that children can practice basic skills in addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division operations. This Math Game project can be used to choose the types of questions and what factors you want to use. This project has three timing options.

 

Random math problems using values ​​from 0 to 9 will be presented. Timing options are provided to measure accuracy and speed.

 

Description

There are many controls used. Two label controls are used for title information, two for displaying scores. There is a wide label in the middle of the form to display math questions. And, long skinny label is used as separator. Two button controls are used to start and stop question and one button to exit the project. There are three group control boxes.

 

Figure 2.1 Controls used in Math Game project

 

The first group box holds four check box controls that are used to select the type of questions. The second group box holds eleven radio buttons that are used to select values ​​that are used as factors in calculations. The third group box contains three radio button controls for timing options. A scroll bar control rod is used to change the time.

 

Run the project (press <F5>). This math game program will be displayed as follows:

 

Figure 2.2 Math Game when first runs

 

Many options are available. First, select the type of question from Type of Question group box. Select addition, subtraction, multiplication, and/or division questions. You can also choose Factor , any value from 0 to 9, or choose Random for random factor. These options can be changed at any time. To start game, click on Start Training button as shown in Figure 2.3.

Step 3

For now, you will ignore the timer option. After this initial code works satisfactorily, the timing issue will be discussed. A step-by-step approach to building a project is always easier than building it all at once.

Here is what happens when Start Training ( btnStart ) button is clicked:

  • Disable Exit button.
  • Set how many questions to be tested and set how many correct answer to zero.

Step 8

You will continue to write the code for generating questions and getting answers (including score) from the user. Then, later you will also learn timer and how to present results.

 

To generate a question, you need to check the latest options selected by user and generate a random question based on those choices. All code will be placed in the function GetQuestion .

 

Look at each step of the question generation process. The first step is to choose a type of random question for a maximum of four possibilities. You will use a simple approach, first generating a random value from 1 to 4 (1 represents addition, 2 for subtraction, 3 for multiplication, and 4 represents division). If the check box (in the Type of Question group box) with the random number is checked, then it will be a type of question. If the check box with the random number is not checked, then you will choose another random value. You continue this process until the type of question is selected. Note this approach assumes that at least one check box is always in the checked position.

After the type of question is selected, you determine the factor used to generate a question. This factor can be a value from 0 to 9, or a random value from 0 to 9, based on the radio button selected in Factor group box.

 

The GetFactor function provides a factor based on radio button selection in the Factor group box and type of question, P . For random factor, this function ensures that zero is not used as a return value if a division problem is being generated.

private int GetFactor( int p)

{

    if (rdoFactor0.Checked)

        return (0);

    else if (rdoFactor1.Checked)

        return (1);

    else if (rdoFactor2.Checked)

        return (2);

    else if (rdoFactor3.Checked)

        return (3);

    else if (rdoFactor4.Checked)

        return (4);

    else if (rdoFactor5.Checked)

        return (5);

    else if (rdoFactor6.Checked)

        return (6);

    else if (rdoFactor7.Checked)

        return (7);

    else if (rdoFactor8.Checked)

        return (8);

    else if (rdoFactor9.Checked)

        return (9);

    else

    {

        // Random

        if (p == 4)

            return (MyRandom.Next(9) + 1);

        else

            return (MyRandom.Next(10));

    }

}

 

If a random option ( rdoFactorRandom ) is selected, 0 to 9 is generated for addition, subtraction, and multiplication problems; 1 to 9 are generated for the division problem (p = 4). In other cases, the selected factor is used as a return value.

private string GetQuestion()

{

    int PType, P, RandValue, Factor;

    P = 0;

 

    do

    {

        PType = MyRandom.Next(4) + 1;

        if (PType == 1 && chkAdd.Checked)

        {

            // Addition

            P = PType;

            RandValue = MyRandom.Next(10);

            Factor = GetFactor(1);

            CorrectAnswer = RandValue + Factor;

            Question = RandValue.ToString() + " + " +

                Factor.ToString() + " = " ;

        }

 

        else if (PType == 2 && chkSubs.Checked)

        {

            // Substraction

            P = PType;

            Factor = GetFactor(2);

            CorrectAnswer = MyRandom.Next(10);

            RandValue = CorrectAnswer + Factor;

            Question = RandValue.ToString() + " - " +

                Factor.ToString() + " = " ;

        }

 

        else if (PType == 3 && chkMul.Checked)

        {

            // Multiplication

            P = PType;

            RandValue = MyRandom.Next(10);

            Factor = GetFactor(3);

            CorrectAnswer = RandValue * Factor;

            Question = RandValue.ToString() + " x " +

                Factor.ToString() + " = " ;

        }

 

        else if (PType == 4 && chkDiv.Checked)

        {

            // Division

            P = PType;

            Factor = GetFactor(4);

            CorrectAnswer = MyRandom.Next(10);

            RandValue = CorrectAnswer * Factor;

            Question = RandValue.ToString() + " / " +

                Factor.ToString() + " = " ;

        }

    } while (P == 0);

 

    if (CorrectAnswer < 10)

    {

        Digits = 1;

        return (Question + "?" );

    }

    else

    {

        Digits = 2;

        return (Question + "??" );

    }

}

Step 11

After a question is displayed, user can enter the digits as the answer. The digits will be entered using the keyboard. Key presses are handled by the KeyPress event of the form. When the form has focus, any key pressed will be interpreted and used.

In form designing, you have set the KeyPreview property of the form to True . This is needed so that all key presses are processed by the KeyPress event, before they are used by other controls. You will also make sure the form has focus when it needs it.

 

The steps for reading and checking answer are as follows:

  • Make sure the pressed key is a value between 0 to 9.
  • If the correct value is entered, then the value will be used as part of the answer to replace the question mark on the question.
  • If the question mark is still left, another key press will be awaited.
  • If all question marks have been replaced, the answer will be compared with the correct answer.
  • Increment the number of the questions that have been tested.
  • If the answer is correct, the number of questions that have been answered correctly will be incremented.
  • Update score label controls.
  • Generate another question.

You need to declare two form-level variables to load user’s answer and the current number of digits of the answer:

private void FormMathGame_KeyPress( object sender, KeyPressEventArgs e)

{

    if (btnStart.Text == "Start Training" )

        return ;

 

    // Only allows 0-9 keys

    if (e.KeyChar >= '0' && e.KeyChar <= '9' ) {

        e.Handled = false ;

        YourAnswer += e.KeyChar;

        lblQuestion.Text = Question + YourAnswer;

 

        if (NumberDigitsAnswer != Digits)

        {

            NumberDigitsAnswer++;

            lblQuestion.Text += "?" ;

            return ;

        }

        else

        {

            Answered++;

 

            // Checks answer

            if (Convert.ToInt32(YourAnswer) == CorrectAnswer) {

                Correct++;

            }

 

            lblTested.Text = Answered.ToString();

            lblTested.Refresh();

            lblCorrect.Text = Correct.ToString();

            lblCorrect.Refresh();

            lblQuestion.Text = GetQuestion();

            lblQuestion.Refresh();

        }

    }

    else

    {

        e.Handled = true ;

    }

}

Step 13

Choosing question types seems quite simple. You only need to check one or a number of check boxes that you want and the questions will be raised. But there are a number of problems here. Until now, nothing prevented the user from unchecking all check boxes, so that no type of question was selected. You must ensure that at least one check box is always selected. And, if the question of division is selected, you cannot allow zero as a factor. You can now write the code to overcome these two problems.

 

You can use a technique where one method can handle multiple events to process checking for check boxes in the Type of Question group box. You will create a method named chkType_CheckedChanged that will handle CheckedChanged event for four check boxes: chkAdd , chkSubs , chkMul , and chkDiv .

 

In this method, the following steps are involved:

  • Determine which check box i checked.
  • Determine how many check boxes are checked.
  • If chkDiv is checked, you need to ensure that zero is not selected as a factor; if 0 is selected by the user as a factor, you need to change that factor to 1. Also, if chDiv is checked, you need to disable rdoFactor0 .
  • If no check box is checked, you need to check the check box that was last selected.
  • Establish focus on the form.

    //If no check box is checked,

    //you need to check the check box that was last selected

    if (NumberCheck == 0)

        CheckClicked.Checked = true ;

    this .Focus();

}

Step 15

After writing down the code for generating questions and checking answers, you will now solve the problem of using timer in this math game project. Until now, you assumed no timer is used. You have two choices for a timer: (1) when the timer is counting forward, which tracks how long you are solving the problem, and (2) when the timer is counting down from a specified value. In both cases, a control ( lblTimer ) will display the time in minute: second format. In the second case, a vertical scroll bar ( vsbTimer ) will be used to set the value. Timing will be controlled by a timer control at intervals of 1 second (1000 milliseconds).

 

You will use a form-level variable ( QuestionTime ) to store the time value (whether the count is forward or backward) in seconds. Add this variable to the general declaration area:

  • If the forward counting ( rdoTimerForward ) is selected, lblTimer will be displayed and vsbTimer will be disabled. The QuestionTime variable is initialized with 0.
  • If the countdown ( rdoTimerBackward ) is selected, lblTimer and vsbTimer will be displayed. The QuestionTime variable is initialized with 30 times the Value property of vsbTimer (30 seconds for each increment).

private string GetTime( int s)

{

    int min, det;

    string ms, ss;

    min = ( int )(s / 60);

    det = s - 60 * min;

    ms = min.ToString();

    ss = det.ToString();

 

    if (det < 10)

        ss = "0" + ss;

    return (ms + ":" + ss);

}

 

This function takes the time ( s ) in seconds and breaks it down into minutes and seconds. Add this new code to your project.

Step 20

When the timer ( timerQuestion ) is enabled, the displayed time ( lblTimer ) will be updated every second using the Interval property with a value of 1000. The displayed time will be incremented if forward count is selected, decremented if backward count is selected.

 

The steps involved in forward counting are as follows:

  • Increment QuestionTime by 1.
  • Display QuestionTime .
  • If QuestionTime is 1800 (30 minutes), question solving is stopped.

 

The steps involved in backward counting are as follows:

  • Decrement QuestionTime by 1.
  • Display QuestionTime .
  • If QuestionTime is 0, question solving is stopped.

private void timerQuestion_Tick( object sender, EventArgs e)

{

   if (rdoTimerForward.Checked)

    {

        QuestionTime++;

        lblTimer.Text = GetTime(QuestionTime);

 

        if (QuestionTime >= 1800)

        {

            btnStart.PerformClick();

            return ;

       }

    }

   else

    {

        QuestionTime--;

        lblTimer.Text = GetTime(QuestionTime);

 

        if (QuestionTime == 0)

        {

            btnStart.PerformClick();

            return ;

        }

   }

   lblTimer.Refresh();

}

private void btnStart_Click( object sender, EventArgs e)

    if (btnStart.Text == "Start Training" )

    {

        btnStart.Text = "Stop Training" ;

        lblCorrect.Text = "0" ;

        {

            if (rdoTimerForward.Checked)

                QuestionTime = 0;

            else

                QuestionTime = 30 * vsbTimer.Value;

 

            lblTimer.Text = GetTime(QuestionTime);

            timerQuestion.Enabled = true ;

        }

 

        blQuestion.Text = GetQuestion();

    }

    else

    {

        grpTimer.Enabled = true ;

        timerQuestion.Enabled = false ;

        btnStart.Text = "Start Training" ;

        btnExit.Enabled = true ;

        lblQuestion.Text = "" ;

 

       if (Answered > 0)

        {

            Score = ( int )(100 * ( double ) (Correct) / Answered);

            Message = "The number of questions tried: " +

                Answered.ToString() + "\r\n" ;

            Message += " The number of questions correctly answered: " +

                Correct.ToString() + " (" + Score.ToString() + "%)"

                + "\r\n" ;

 

            if (rdoTimerOff.Checked)

            {

                Message += "Timer Off" ;

            }

            else

            {

                if (rdoTimerBackward.Checked)

                {

                    QuestionTime =

                        30 * vsbTimer.Value - QuestionTime;

                }

 

                Message += "Total time spent: " +

                    GetTime(QuestionTime) + "\r\n" ;

                Message += "Average time every question: " +

                    String.Format( "{0:f2}" ,

                    ( double )(QuestionTime) / Answered) + " seconds" ;

            }

 

            MessageBox.Show(Message, "Results" ,

                MessageBoxButtons.OK, MessageBoxIcon.Information);

        }

    }

}

       private void btnExit_Click( object sender, EventArgs e)

        {

            this .Close();

        }

 

        private int GetFactor( int p)

        {

            if (rdoFactor0.Checked)

                return (0);

            else if (rdoFactor1.Checked)

                return (1);

            else if (rdoFactor2.Checked)

                return (2);

            else if (rdoFactor3.Checked)

                return (3);

            else if (rdoFactor4.Checked)

                return (4);

            else if (rdoFactor5.Checked)

                return (5);

            else if (rdoFactor6.Checked)

                return (6);

            else if (rdoFactor7.Checked)

                return (7);

            else if (rdoFactor8.Checked)

                return (8);

            else if (rdoFactor9.Checked)

                return (9);

            else

            {

                // Random

                if (p == 4)

                    return (MyRandom.Next(9) + 1);

                else

                    return (MyRandom.Next(10));

            }

        }

 

        private string GetQuestion()

        {

            int PType, P, RandValue, Factor;

            P = 0;

 

            do

            {

                PType = MyRandom.Next(4) + 1;

                if (PType == 1 && chkAdd.Checked)

                {

                    // Addition

                    P = PType;

                    RandValue = MyRandom.Next(10);

                    Factor = GetFactor(1);

                    CorrectAnswer = RandValue + Factor;

                    Question = RandValue.ToString() + " + "

                        + Factor.ToString() + " = " ;

                }

 

                else if (PType == 2 && chkSubs.Checked)

                {

                    // Substraction

                    P = PType;

                    Factor = GetFactor(2);

                    CorrectAnswer = MyRandom.Next(10);

                    RandValue = CorrectAnswer + Factor;

                    Question = RandValue.ToString() + " - " +

                        Factor.ToString() + " = " ;

                }

 

                else if (PType == 3 && chkMul.Checked)

                {

                    // Multiplication

                    P = PType;

                    RandValue = MyRandom.Next(10);

                    Factor = GetFactor(3);

                    CorrectAnswer = RandValue * Factor;

                    Question = RandValue.ToString() + " x " +

                        Factor.ToString() + " = " ;

                }

 

                else if (PType == 4 && chkDiv.Checked)

                {

                    // Division

                    P = PType;

                    Factor = GetFactor(4);

                    CorrectAnswer = MyRandom.Next(10);

                    RandValue = CorrectAnswer * Factor;

                    Question = RandValue.ToString() + " / " +

                        Factor.ToString() + " = " ;

                }

            } while (P == 0);

 

            YourAnswer = "" ;

            NumberDigitsAnswer = 1;

            this .Focus();

 

            if (CorrectAnswer < 10)

            {

                Digits = 1;

                return (Question + "?" );

            }

            else

            {

                Digits = 2;

                return (Question + "??" );

            }

        }

 

        private void FormMathGame_KeyPress( object sender, KeyPressEventArgs e)

        {

            if (btnStart.Text == "Start Training" )

                return ;

 

            // Only allows 0-9 keys

            if (e.KeyChar >= '0' && e.KeyChar <= '9' ) {

                e.Handled = false ;

                YourAnswer += e.KeyChar;

                lblQuestion.Text = Question + YourAnswer;

 

                if (NumberDigitsAnswer != Digits)

                {

                    NumberDigitsAnswer++;

                    lblQuestion.Text += "?" ;

                    return ;

                }

                else

                {

                    Answered++;

 

                    // Checks answer

                    if (Convert.ToInt32(YourAnswer) == CorrectAnswer) {

                        Correct++;

                    }

 

                    lblTested.Text = Answered.ToString();

                    lblTested.Refresh();

                    lblCorrect.Text = Correct.ToString();

                    lblCorrect.Refresh();

                    lblQuestion.Text = GetQuestion();

                    lblQuestion.Refresh();

                }

            }

            else

            {

                e.Handled = true ;

            }

        }

 

        private void chkType_CheckedChanged( object sender, EventArgs e)

        {

            CheckBox CheckClicked;          

            int NumberCheck;

 

            // Determines which checkbox is selected

            CheckClicked = (CheckBox)sender;

 

            // Determines how many check boxes are checked

            NumberCheck = 0;

            if (chkAdd.Checked)

                NumberCheck++;

            if (chkSubs.Checked)

                NumberCheck++;

            if (chkMul.Checked)

                NumberCheck++;

            if (chkDiv.Checked)

            {

                NumberCheck++;

 

                // Ensures that zero is not selected as a factor

                if (rdoFactor0.Checked)

                    rdoFactor1.PerformClick();

 

                rdoFactor0.Enabled = false ;

            }

            else

            {

                rdoFactor0.Enabled = true ;

            }

 

            //If no check box is checked,

            //you need to check the check box that was last selected

 

            if (NumberCheck == 0)

                CheckClicked.Checked = true ;

            this .Focus();

        }

 

        private void rdoTimer_CheckedChanged( object sender, EventArgs e)

        {

            if (rdoTimerOff.Checked)

            {

                lblTimer.Visible = false ;

                vsbTimer.Visible = false ;

            }

            else if (rdoTimerForward.Checked)

            {

                QuestionTime = 0;

                lblTimer.Text = GetTime(QuestionTime);

                lblTimer.Visible = true ;

                vsbTimer.Visible = false ;

            }

            else if (rdoTimerBackward.Checked)

            {

                QuestionTime = 30 * vsbTimer.Value;

                lblTimer.Text = GetTime(QuestionTime);

                lblTimer.Visible = true ;

                vsbTimer.Visible = true ;

            }

        }

 

        private string GetTime( int s)

        {

            int min, det;

            string ms, ss;

            min = ( int )(s / 60);

            det = s - 60 * min;

            ms = min.ToString();

            ss = det.ToString();

 

            if (det < 10)

                ss = "0" + ss;

            return (ms + ":" + ss);

        }

 

        private void vsbTimer_Scroll( object sender, ScrollEventArgs e)

        {

            lblTimer.Text = GetTime(30 * vsbTimer.Value);

            lblTimer.Refresh();

        }

 

        private void timerQuestion_Tick( object sender, EventArgs e)

        {

            if (rdoTimerForward.Checked)

            {

                QuestionTime++;

                lblTimer.Text = GetTime(QuestionTime);

 

                if (QuestionTime >= 1800)

                {

                    btnStart.PerformClick();

                    return ;

                }

            }

            else

            {

                QuestionTime--;

                lblTimer.Text = GetTime(QuestionTime);

 

                if (QuestionTime == 0)

                {

                    btnStart.PerformClick();

                    return ;

                }

            }

            lblTimer.Refresh();

        }

    }

}

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

TUTORIAL 3

BANK CODE

 

In this tutorial, you will build Bank Code game. The storage box is locked and can only be opened if you enter the correct digit combination. Combinations can be 2 to 4 non-repetitive digits (range of digits from 1 to 9). After a guess is given, you will be notified of how many digits are right and how many digits are in the right position. Based on this information, you will give another guess. You continue to guess until you get the right combination or until you stop the game.

 

 

Description

On the left side of the form is a large picture box control. On the right side, two group box controls and two button controls are placed. In the picture box, a control panel is placed. In the panel, there are four label controls (set the AutoSize property to False ) and nine button controls. In the first group box control, place three radio buttons. In the second group box control, a text box control is placed.

 

Figure 3.1 All controls used in Bank Code project

 

The picture box contains an image of bank and a panel. The label controls in the panel are used to display the combinations entered (the BorderStyle property set to FixedSingle to display the label size). The nine buttons on the panel are used to enter combinations. Radio buttons are used to set options. The buttons (one to start and stop the game and another to exit the project) are used to control game operations. The text box displays the results of the combinations entered.

 

Figure 3.2 User chooses 3 Digits Combination and clicks Start Game button

 

Figure 3.3 User guesses three digits and the result displayed on text box control

 

Run the project (press <F5>). The game will be displayed in a "stop" state. You can then choose the combination option 2, 3, or 4 digits. If you choose a 3 digit combination and click Start Game button, it will appear as shown in Figure 3.2

 

Because 3 digits combination option is selected, only three labels are displayed to enter the combination. Now you can select the three digit guesses by pressing the number keys provided. After you select the guess, the results will be displayed in the text box to the right of the form as shown in Figure 3.3.

When the user clicks Start Game button in the "stop" state, several things happen to switch the game to the "play" state:

  • Determine the secret combination.
  • Check whether the input matches a secret combination.
  • Display the results.

Step 12

The critical step in this project is to generate the secret combination that the player will guess. With the options selected, you know that combinations can be 2 to 4 digits. You also specify that there are no repetitive digits in the combination.

 

Because repetitive digits is not allowed, for each digit in combination, you generate a random number from 1 to 9, but only add it to the combination if the random value has not been used before. Here is a code snippet to do this task:

 

1

// Determines combination

SecretCombo = "" ;

int j;

bool UniqueDigit;

for ( int i = 0; i < NumberOfDigit; i++)

{

    // Chooses unique digit

    do

    {

        j = MyRandom.Next(9) + 1;

        UniqueDigit = true ;

        if (i != 0)

        {

            for ( int k = 0; k < i; k++)

            {

                if (SecretCombo[k].ToString() == j.ToString())

                     UniqueDigit = false ;

            }

        }

    }

    while (!UniqueDigit);

    SecretCombo += j.ToString();

}

 

In the code above, a string variable ( SecretCombo ) is used to store a combination. Initially this variable is empty. One digit at a time ( numberDigits ) is added to the SecretCombo using string splicing.

 

A random digit J (from 1 to 9) is raised. You then look at the latest digit in the code to check whether the newly generated digit is a digit unit. If so, the digit is added to the SecretCombo . If it is not unique, a new random digit will be raised. All of this logic is implemented in loop Do . Learn how Mid function is used to see individual digits in SecretCombo .

Step 16

You are now ready to accept the player's guess to guess the secret combination using 9 keypad buttons. You can just write a Click event method for each of these buttons to get user input. Or, you can implement smarter steps by using an event method to handle clicking on the nine key controls.

 

After the secret combination is raised, the next step is to let the user enter his guess. This is done using 9 number keys on the pnlBank control. The steps are as follows:

  • Read the digits entered by the user.
  • If this is the first digit of a combination, all previous guesses are deleted on label controls.
  • Determine which button clicked.
  • Disable buttons that are clicked due to repeated digits is not permitted.
  • Add number in Text property of the button that was clicked into the user input combination.
  • Display the number on the corresponding label control.
  • If all digits have been entered, the buttons are enabled again and user input is compared with the actual secret combination. If not, repeat the steps above.

 

The code to perform these steps is placed in a method called btnCombo_Click . This method is to handle the Click event for the nine buttons for user input ( btn1 through btn9 ).

private void btnCombo_Click( object sender, EventArgs e)

{

    String n;

 

    // Determines which button clicked

    Button ButtonClicked;

    ButtonClicked = (Button) sender;

 

    // Text property of clicked button

    // If first button clicekd, clear all labels

    if (DigitEntered == 0)

    {

        Combo[0].Text = "" ;

        Combo[1].Text = "" ;

        Combo[2].Text = "" ;

        Combo[3].Text = "" ;

    }

 

    // Add Text property of clicked button in ComboEntered

    ComboEntered += n;

    DigitEntered++;

    Combo[DigitEntered - 1].Text = n;

 

    // If all digits has been entered, check combination

    if (DigitEntered == NumberOfDigit)

    {

        // Resets combination buttons

        for ( int i = 0; i < 9; i++)

            ComboButton[i].Enabled = true ;

 

        // Checks combination

        Console.WriteLine(ComboEntered);

    }

}

Step 21

You now have the capability to generate a combination of secrets and read user's guesses. You need code that compares two string variables and displays the results. If it matches, it means the user has managed to guess the secret combination. If not, the user will be notified of how many digits are right and how many digits are in the right position.

 

After the user has finished entering the guess, these steps need to be carried out:

  • Display the user's guess ( ComboEntered ) in the textResult .
  • If the user's guess ( ComboEntered ) is the same as the secret combination ( SecretCombo ), then the game will be switched to the "stop" state.
  • If the guess is incorrect, number of exact digits and number of digits that are in the right position will be determined. Then, this information is displayed in the textResult control.
  • Clear user's guess for the next guess.

 

The code to implement these steps is placed in the Click event method of the btnCombo control:

private void btnCombo_Click( object sender, EventArgs e)

{

    String n;

    int CorrectDigits, CorrectPositions;

 

    // Determines which button clicked

    Button ButtonClicked;

    ButtonClicked = (Button) sender;

 

    // Text property of clicked button

    n = ButtonClicked.Text;

 

    // Disables clicked button

    ButtonClicked.Enabled = false ;

 

    // If first button clicekd, clear all labels

    if (DigitEntered == 0)

    {

        Combo[0].Text = "" ;

        Combo[1].Text = "" ;

        Combo[2].Text = "" ;

        Combo[3].Text = "" ;

    }

 

    // Add Text property of clicked button in ComboEntered

    ComboEntered += n;

    DigitEntered++;

    Combo[DigitEntered - 1].Text = n;

 

    // If all digits has been entered, check combination

    if (DigitEntered == NumberOfDigit)

    {

        // Resets combination buttons

        for ( int i = 0; i < 9; i++)

            ComboButton[i].Enabled = true ;

 

        // Checks combination

        textResult.AppendText( "Entered: " +

            ComboEntered + "\r\n" );

        if (ComboEntered == SecretCombo)

            btnStartStop.PerformClick();

        else

        {

            CorrectDigits = 0;

            for ( int i = 0; i < NumberOfDigit; i++)

            {

                n = ComboEntered[i].ToString();

                for ( int j = 0; j < NumberOfDigit; j++)

                    if (n == SecretCombo[j].ToString())

                        CorrectDigits++;

            }

 

            // Number of digits in correct position

            CorrectPositions = 0;

            for ( int i = 0; i < NumberOfDigit; i++)

                if (SecretCombo[i] == ComboEntered[i])

                    CorrectPositions++;

            textResult.AppendText(CorrectDigits.ToString() +

                " correct digits" + "\r\n" );

            textResult.AppendText(CorrectPositions.ToString() +

                " in correct position" + "\r\n" );

            textResult.AppendText( "Please try again ..." +

                "\r\n\r\n" );

 

            // Clears combination

            ComboEntered = "" ;

            DigitEntered = 0;   

       }

    }

}

 

The above code first counts the exact digits of the user input. The Code that checks if the digits are in the right position compares each digit in ComboEntered and SecretCombo . All results are displayed in the text box.

The code is used to distinguish game termination before guessing the combination from game termination because the secret combination has been guessed.

private void btnStartStop_Click( object sender, EventArgs e)

{

    if (btnStartStop.Text == "Start Game" )

    {

        btnStartStop.Text = "Stop Game" ;

        grpOption.Enabled = false ;

        btnExit.Enabled = false ;

        pnlBank.Enabled = true ;

        textResult.Text = "" ;

 

        // Determines number of digits in combination           

        if (rdoTwoDigits.Checked)

        {

            NumberOfDigit = 2;

        }

        else if (rdoThreeDigits.Checked)

        {

            NumberOfDigit = 3;

        }

        else

        {

            NumberOfDigit = 4;

        }

 

        for ( int i = 0; i < NumberOfDigit; i++)

        {

            Combo[i].Visible = true ;

            Combo[i].Text = "" ;

        }

 

        if (NumberOfDigit != 4)

        {

            for ( int i = NumberOfDigit; i < 4; i++)

            {

                Combo[i].Visible = false ;

            }

        }

 

        // Determines combination

        SecretCombo = "" ;

        int j;

        bool UniqueDigit;

        for ( int i = 0; i < NumberOfDigit; i++)

        {

            // Chooses unique digit

            do

            {

                j = MyRandom.Next(9) + 1;

                UniqueDigit = true ;

                if (i != 0)

                {

                    for ( int k = 0; k < i; k++)

                    {

                        if ( SecretCombo[k].ToString() == j.ToString())

                            UniqueDigit = false ;

                    }

                }

            }

            while (!UniqueDigit);

            SecretCombo += j.ToString();

        }

        ComboEntered = "" ;

        DigitEntered = 0;

    }

    else

    {

        if (ComboEntered == SecretCombo)

            textResult.AppendText( "Correct!!!!" + "\r\n" );

        else

            textResult.AppendText( "Game Stopped" + "\r\n" );

        textResult.AppendText( "Combination: " + SecretCombo);

 

        btnStartStop.Text = "Start Game" ;

        grpOption.Enabled = true ;

        btnExit.Enabled = true ;

        pnlBank.Enabled = false ;

    }

}

TUTORIAL 4

HORSE RACING

 

 

In this tutorial, you will build Horse Racing game. This is a simple game. Up to 10 horses will race to the finish line. You guessed two horses that you thought could win the race. By clicking on the Start button, the race will start. All horses will race speed to get to the finish line.

 

 

Description

Labels are used to display instructions and number of horses in a race. Four button controls are used: two buttons to change number of horses, one button to start the game, and one other button to stop the game. The picture box control is used to load the horse image. A timer control is used to update the horse's movement during the race.

 

Figure 4.1 All controls used in Horse Racing game project

 

Run the program (press <F5>). The game will run in the 'initial' state. The program description and instructions will be displayed. At this point, the user can click Start button to start the game, click the arrow button to change number of horses to be competed or click Stop to stop the program.

 

Figure 4.2 The Horse Racing game is at initial state showing program description and instructions

 

 

Change number of horses if you want (for example, 8) by clicking the right arrow button under Number of Horses . Click Start button to start the game. Program instructions will disappear. Eight horses will be displayed, ready to race:

 

Figure 4.3 Eight horses are ready to race

 

In this situation, the user needs to choose two horses that are considered to win the race. To do this, the user only needs to click on the desired horses using mouse, and a red X symbol will be displayed next to the selected horses, as shown in Figure 4.4.

 

Figure 4.4 Two red X symbols will appear when user choose two horses guessed to win race

 

Then, the user can click on the Start button to start the race. All horses race across the screen to reach the finish line:

 

Figure 4.5 All horses race to finish line when user clicks Start button

Step 1

You will start building Horse Racing game project. Start a new project in Visual Basic. It is recommended that you immediately save it with a name that you choose yourself. This will create the folders and file structure needed for your project.

 

Step 2

Place two panel controls on the form (one panel with a width of 100 pixels on the left side, one other panel with a width of 900 pixels on the right side). Place two labels and four buttons in the left panel. Place a label control and a picture box control in the right panel. Add a timer control. The form will now look as shown in Figure 4.6.

 

Labels are used to display information. Two buttons are used to change number of horses, two other buttons to start and stop the game. The timer control sets the horse's movements.

    if (StatusGame == "Start" ) // Decreases number of horses

    {

       NumberOfHorses -= 1;

       if (NumberOfHorses < 3)

            NumberOfHorses = 3;

 

        lblHorse.Text = NumberOfHorses.ToString();

    }

}

 

private void btnRight_Click( object sender, EventArgs e)

{

    if (StatusGame == "Start" ) // Decreases number of horses

   {

        NumberOfHorses += 1;

       if (NumberOfHorses >10)

            NumberOfHorses = 10;

 

        lblHorse.Text = NumberOfHorses.ToString();

   }

}

 

This code is quite simple. Number of horses is only changed when the game is in the "Start" state. If the < button is clicked, the program will reduce number of horses by one (with a minimum of 3). If the > button is clicked, the program will add number of horses by one (with a maximum of 10). New value ​​for number of horses is then displayed.

Step 11

After the game is in the "Stop" condition, the user can choose two horses that he wants to compete to reach finish line. To detect click on a horse, you need to know its location and size. From the code that places the horse on pnlGame , you can see for i-th horse (where i starts from 1 to NumberOfHorses ):

 

1

The HorsesChosenArr is used to tell which horses are selected. A red X will be placed next to the selected horse. After two horses are selected ( NumberOfHorsesByUser = 2), you can start the race by clicking Start . If the user clicks on two horses and wants to change the race, the user can click on the horse which has been deleted and the red X will disappear so the user can choose another.

 

When a horse is clicked, the following steps are taken:

  • If the horse has been selected before, then NumberOfHorsesByUser is decremented, set HorsesChosenArr[i] to 0 and delete the letter X next to the horse.
  • If the horse is not selected before and NumberOfHorsesByUser is less than 2, then NumberOfHorsesByUser is incremented, set HorsesChosenArr[i] to 1 and draw a red X next to the horse.

You follow these steps in that order to ensure that the user does not click on a horse that has been previously selected.

private void pnlGame_MouseDown( object sender, MouseEventArgs e)

{

   int HorseClicked;

 

    if (StatusGame == "Stop" )

    {

       //User chooses two horses

        Decimal ValHorses = (e.Y - 10)/60;

        HorseClicked = Convert.ToInt32(Math.Floor(ValHorses) + 1);

 

        //if horse has been clicked before, delete letter X

        if (HorsesChosenArr[HorseClicked] == 1)

        {

           NumberOfHorsesByUser -= 1;

            HorsesChosenArr[HorseClicked] = 0;

            PanelGame.FillRectangle(Brushes.White, 10,

                (HorseClicked - 1) * 60 + 20, 30, 30);

        }

 

        else if (NumberOfHorsesByUser < 2)

        {

            //If the horse is not selected before

            NumberOfHorsesByUser += 1;

            HorsesChosenArr[HorseClicked] = 1;

            PanelGame.DrawLine(Pens.Red, 10,

                (HorseClicked - 1) * 60 + 20, 40,

                (HorseClicked - 1) * 60 + 50);

            PanelGame.DrawLine(Pens.Red, 10,

                (HorseClicked - 1) * 60 + 50, 40,

                (HorseClicked - 1) * 60 + 20);

       }

    }

}

Step 13

After two horses are selected, user can click on Start button to start the race, which puts the game into "Moving" state. So, when Start button is clicked in the "Stop" state, the following steps will be performed:

  • Change StatusGame to "Move".
  • Clear instructions.
  • For each horse, the final random position is determined before the finish line.
  • Two winners are chosen at random.
  • Move horses to their final positions.
  • Change StatusGame to "Start" before another race starts.

 

To move a horse, you use the timer control ( timerHorse ). With each Tick event, you move each horse as far as a fraction of the difference between its starting and ending position. This method gives a smooth animation to the final position in 5000 milliseconds (5 seconds). Because the interval is 100 milliseconds, you move each horse for 1/50 times the difference between the starting and ending positions for each Click event. You can change this value.

private void btnStart_Click( object sender, EventArgs e)

{

    if (StatusGame == "Start" ) //User clicks Start button

    {

        StatusGame = "Stop" ;

        lblInstruction.Visible = false ;

 

        PanelGame.Clear(Color.White); //Draws horse and trajectory

        for ( int i = 1; i <= NumberOfHorses; i++)

        {

            PanelGame.DrawImage(picHorse.Image, 50,

                (i - 1) * 60 + 10);

            PanelGame.DrawLine(Pens.Green, 50, (i - 1) * 60 + 35,

                820, (i - 1) * 60 + 35);

        }

 

        //Draws finisih line

        PanelGame.FillRectangle(Brushes.Pink, 820, 10, 10,

            NumberOfHorses * 60 - 10);

        Font MyFont = new Font( "Arial" , 14);

        PanelGame.DrawString( "Click on the two horses you choose." ,

            MyFont, Brushes.Red, 200, 40);

        PanelGame.DrawString( " Click the Start button to start the race. " ,

            MyFont, Brushes.Red, 200, 70);

 

        NumberOfHorsesByUser = 0;

 

        for ( int i = 1; i <= NumberOfHorses; i++)

            HorsesChosenArr[i] = 0;

    }

 

    else if (StatusGame == "Stop" && NumberOfHorsesByUser == 2){

       StatusGame = "Moving" ;

       PanelGame.FillRectangle(Brushes.White, 150, 40, 450, 50);

 

        //Determines starting position/final position

        NumberOfMoves = 0;

        for ( int i = 1; i <= NumberOfHorses; i++)

       {

            HorsePosition[i] = 50;

            LastPosition[i] = 400 + MyRandom.Next(360);

       }

 

        //Chooses two winners

        Winner[0] = MyRandom.Next(NumberOfHorses) + 1;

 

   NextWinner:

       Winner[1] = MyRandom.Next(NumberOfHorses) + 1;

 

        if (Winner[0] == Winner[1])

            goto NextWinner;

 

        LastPosition[Winner[0]] = 850;

        LastPosition[Winner[1]] = 850;

        timerHorse.Start();

    }

}

private void timerHorse_Tick( object sender, EventArgs e)

{

    NumberOfMoves += 1;

 

   for ( int i = 1; i <= NumberOfHorses; i++)

    {

        PanelGame.FillRectangle(Brushes.White,

            HorsePosition[i], (i - 1) * 60 + 10, 50, 50);

        HorsePosition[i] += (LastPosition[i] - 50) / 50;

        PanelGame.DrawImage(picHorse.Image,

            HorsePosition[i], (i - 1) * 60 + 10);

   }

 

    if (NumberOfMoves == 49)

    {

        timerHorse.Stop();

        StatusGame = "Start" ;

    }

}

TUTORIAL 6

CATCHING BALL GAME

 

In this tutorial, you will build Catching Ball game. The bird flew and dropped ball from the sky. Users are challenged to position man under the fallen ball to catch it.

 

 

Description

Labels are used for instructions and to display game information (remaining time, number of balls captured, and game difficulty level). Two buttons are used to change the game difficulty level, one button to start the game, and another button to stop the game. Picture box controls hold images for man, bird, and ball.

 

Run the program (press <F5>). The game will appear in the "starting" state. Description and program instructions are given. At this point, the user can click Start button to start the game, click the arrow buttons to change the difficulty level of the game or click Stop button to stop the program.

 

Figure 3.1 All controls used in Catching Ball game project

 

Figure 6.2 The Catcing Ball game is at “starting” state showing program description and instructions

 

Change the game's difficulty level if desired (for example 5) by clicking on the small arrow buttons below Difficulty label. Then click on Start button. Program instructions will disappear. A bird is displayed above the screen dropping ball. This is the "playing" state:

 

Figure 6.3 Game is at “playing” state

 

You can shift or move man to below the ball to catch it. You can move man using the arrow keys on the keyboard or by pressing the left or right mouse button. When the ball reaches man, you will get one point. If the ball is not captured and passes man, the score does not increase:

 

Figure 6.4 User can move man to below the ball to catch it, using arrow keys on the keyboard or by pressing the left or right mouse button

 

 

Figure 6.5 Final result is displayed in a message box

The game continues for 60 seconds. Remaining time is displayed. And the final result is displayed in the message box that appears at the end of the game, as shown in Figure 6.5.

 

 

Tutorial Steps

Step 1

You will start building Catching Ball game project, by designing the form. Start a new project in Visual Basic. Once started, it is recommended that you save the project with the name you choose. This will create the folder and file structure needed for your project.

 

Place two control panels on the form (one panel with a width of 100 pixels on the left side and one other panel with a width of 900 pixels on the right side). Make the two panels have a height of 600 pixels. Place six labels and four buttons in the left panel. Place a label control and three picture box controls on the right panel. Add a timer control. The form will look like this:

 

Figure 6.6 All controls user and their positions form

 

The labels on the left panel are used to display game information. Two buttons are used to change the game difficulty level, one button to start the game, and one other button to stop the game. The label controls on the right panel are used to display game instructions. Picture boxes are used to contain Man, Bird, and Ball images. Timer is used to control the game.
